elements.quote: Editorials, commentaries, opinion papers, conference abstracts, media reports, letters, bulletins, pre-prints, grey literature, non-English language studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses were excluded from the search.

elements.quote: a comprehensive search across PubMed and Embase databases was performed of peer-reviewed literature published from inception until June 2024.

elements.quote: The search yielded 2950 records, of which 15 met the inclusion criteria. The studies were carried out mainly in countries in Africa (53.3%), ... The most used interventions for analyses were insecticide-treated bed nets (93.3%), IRS (80.0%), Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention (33.3%) and Case management (33.3%).
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (15) and summarizes study characteristics, but it does not report the total number of participants across included studies.

elements.quote: The most used interventions for analyses were insecticide-treated bed nets (93.3%), IRS (80.0%), Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention (33.3%) and Case management (33.3%). The methods used for estimating health benefits were compartmental models (40.0%), individual-based models (40.0%), static models (13.0%) and linear regression model (7%).
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for the main outcomes of interest in the review (e.g., frequency of interventions analyzed and model types), including numbers/percentages for these outcomes.

elements.reason: No meta-analysis was conducted (the manuscript reports a narrative synthesis), so reporting a summary estimate and interval is not applicable.

elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings and assess their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: The abstract does not report any group comparisons with direction of effect; it summarizes study characteristics and findings rather than comparative effect estimates, so this item is not applicable.
The abstract does not briefly summarize important limitations of the included evidence (e.g., risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision).

elements.quote: The findings highlighted the need for country-specific analysis for malaria control optimization, the use of country-specific epidemiological and cost data in performing modelling analyses, performing cost sensitivity analyses and defining the perspective for the analysis, with an emphasis on subnational tailoring for data collection and analysis for more accurate and good quality results. It is critical that the future modelling efforts account for fairness and target at risk malaria populations that are hard-to-reach to maximize impact.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results and their important implications for future modelling and policy.
The abstract does not state the primary source of funding for the review.

elements.quote: There is limited evidence in peer-reviewed literature on modelling for malaria optimization in limited resource settings. The country focus of the modelling studies included in the review were not representative of the burden of malaria in sub-Saharan Africa. ... The limited number of modelling analyses for malaria control optimization specific to countries within Africa and Asia is as a consequence of the lack or inaccessibility of country-specific epidemiologic and cost data at the national and subnational levels. This data gap limits future studies within the respective countries, limits the build-up of a critical mass of modellers within these countries, and makes it challenging for policymakers to make an evidence-based informed case to potential donors for future funding.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the current state of knowledge and specific important uncertainties and data gaps (limited evidence, non-representative country focus, lack of country-specific epidemiologic and cost data) relevant to modelling for malaria optimization.

elements.quote: Background Despite advances made in curbing the global malaria burden since the 2000s, progress has stalled, in part due to a plateauing of the financing available to implement needed interventions. In 2020, approximately 3.3 billion USD was invested globally for malaria interventions, falling short of the targeted 6.8 billion USD set by the GTS, increasing the financial gap between desirable and actual investment. Models for malaria control optimization are used to disentangle the most efficient interventions or packages of interventions for inherently constrained budgets. This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings and assess their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: The abstract and background explain the importance and need for the review (stalled progress, financing gap) and state that models help identify efficient interventions for constrained budgets, justifying the review.
No evidence in the provided text that the authors identified, discussed, or cited previous similar systematic reviews or explained the need relative to existing reviews.

The item applies 'for reviews of intervention effects.' This review is of models for optimisation/resource allocation rather than a review of intervention effects, so describing mechanisms of action is not applicable based on the provided evidence.

The requirement to consider a logic model applies to complex interventions or delivery contexts; the provided evidence presents a modelling methods review and does not present or report a logic model, and the review focus (model characterisation/optimization) makes this item not applicable in the provided text.

elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings and assess their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: The abstract gives an explicit statement of the review objective: to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited-resource settings and to assess their strengths and limitations. The research question in methods further clarifies the focus on publications describing how models have been used to allocate resources.

The review addresses models for resource allocation rather than comparing intervention effects; the stated research question and objective focus on identifying and characterising optimization models for allocating resources (text_6 and text_2), so specifying planned comparisons using PICO for intervention effects is not applicable.

elements.quote: This manuscript provides a systematic review of existing literature to identify models for malaria control optimization. However, the review has certain limitations, which are outlined below: The review did not include abstracts from scientific conferences or other scientific meetings, potentially omitting important modelling studies conducted by national malaria control programs (NMCPs) to inform resource allocation decisions. And so, although the findings from this review shows that there are relatively few published modelling studies or examples that incorporate cost constraints and describe how to optimize limited budgets, the findings from this manuscript may not fully represent the actual use of models for malaria control optimization worldwide. The absence of these studies from the review limits the comprehensiveness of the findings, suggesting a need for the development of additional approaches to better capture and reflect the full range of modelling activities being undertaken globally.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly includes a 'Limitations' section that discusses limitations of the evidence included in the review, including exclusion of conference abstracts and potential incompleteness of captured modelling activities.

elements.quote: The findings highlighted the need for country-specific modelling analysis for malaria control optimization, country-specific epidemiological and cost data for analysis, performing cost sensitivity analyses and defining the perspective for the analysis, with an emphasis on subnational tailoring for data collection and analysis for more accurate and good quality results. Such efforts should include all efficient prevention and treatment interventions, and surveillance and vaccination to inform context-specific control and elimination efforts respectively. It is critical that the future modelling efforts account for equity considerations and target at risk malaria populations that are hard-to-reach to maximize impact.
